newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: N.Korea sees war as exit from crisis - defector.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea sees war as exit from crisis - defector.

text.p: The highest ranking North Korean ever to flee his homeland said on Thursday that leader Kim Jong-il was preparing for war, but that he had no proof Pyongyang had nuclear weapons.
Hwang Jang-yop said Kim had rejected reform and was planning a lightning assault to capture the South within days as the only escape from his country's dire straits.
"The North's war preparation is beyond imagination," he said, describing the entire country as a fortress with tunnels and underground military facilities.
Hwang advised the South to stand tough.

"The bad guys should be dealt with in a strong manner. Kennedy averted a nuclear war by taking a strong stand against Khrushchev," he said, referring to a Cold War-era showdown between U.S. president John F. Kennedy and Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev during the 1960s Cuban missile crisis.

On arrival in Seoul on April 20, Hwang declared his mission was to stop Pyongyang from launching war. And he caused a sensation by warning that Pyongyang could "scorch" South Korea, and even Japan, in a nuclear attack.
But on Thursday, after several months of debriefing by South Korean and U.S. intelligence officials, Hwang conceded he had no concrete evidence to back up his nuclear claims.
"It is common knowledge they do have these weapons, but there is no means to verify that," he said. Nevertheless, he said it "would be wise" to assume the worst.

Western intelligence officials had cast doubt on whether Hwang, an ideologue who helped to author Pyongyang's guiding ideology of self-reliance, or "juche", was in a position to reveal North Korea's nuclear secrets.
Hwang sought asylum at South Korea's Beijing consulate in February, and was stuck for more than two months in China and the Philippines before being spirited to Seoul.

Hwang said Kim Jong-il had been in full control since the death of his father, "Great Leader" Kim Il-sung, in 1994. He portrayed the son as a cruel dictator who would not compromise his power to rescue his country from a "living hell".
Kim Jong-il had been tightening his grip on the military as Pyongyang gradually lost control of the movement of citizens searching for food.
"The fact that there is nothing to believe in except the military means you have reached the final stage," Hwang said when asked if the Kim Jong-il regime would collapse.

But he brushed aside speculation that there might be divisions between moderates and hardliners in the North, or groups opposing Kim. "It is a country of one-man dictatorship. Kim Jong-il makes all decisons and policies. There is no other power," he said.
He predicted that Kim Jong-il would formally assume leadership of the all-powerful Workers' Party this year.
North Korea on Tuesday declared an end to a three-year mourning period for Kim Il-sung, paving the way for the son to assume the vacant posts of Workers' Party general secretary and state president.
Kim Jong-il would take over as general secretary after the hot summer, when ceremonies would be easier to arrange, and be named president either this year or next, Hwang said.

He said Kim knew that a drawn-out war would spell defeat for the North, but was ready to launch a surprise attack if there was internal turmoil in the South or the United States was sidetracked with conflicts elsewhere.

Last year's grounding of a North Korean submarine with 26 commandos on a Southern beach was an "unfortunate incident" for Pyongyang, which had sent many other submarines on spy missions in the past, Hwang said.
